newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu meets Egypt envoy, PLO irked by report.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu meets Egypt envoy, PLO irked by report.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu held talks with an Egyptian peace envoy on Thursday to seek ways to revive Israeli-PLO peacemaking bogged down for more than two months over Jewish settlement building in the West Bank.

But Palestinian outrage over an Israeli newspaper report that Prime Minister Netanyahu planned to offer the PLO only about 40 percent of the disputed West Bank in a final peace deal underscored the depth of the peace crisis.

"We are making a joint effort, Israel and Egypt, to try and move the political process," Netanyahu told reporters before meeting Egyptian envoy Osama al-Baz. "I hope that this effort will bear fruit."
Netanyahu's office said in a statement that al-Baz briefed Netanyahu on his meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday, adding that the talks were "positive".

The Palestinian reaction to the Haaretz newspaper report of a secret Netanyahu plan to hold onto 60 percent of the West Bank -- where the PLO expects that a final accord due to be completed by May 1999 will give them a state -- was anything but positive.

"These numbers -- excuse the expression -- are political masturbation by the government of Israel," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israeli army radio, suggesting Israelis should negotiate with the Palestinians rather than juggling figures among themselves.

Netanyahu acknowledged in radio interviews having some ideas about a final peace deal and said they were discussed in his inner cabinet for the first time on Wednesday when the military presented its security assessments.
But he said: "I haven't shown anyone or drafted any map."
Haaretz published a detailed front-page illustration of what it called "Netanyahu's map". Asked if he had a map, Netanyahu told Israel Radio: "A map in the head? Who doesn't have one?"

Israel already has handed over much of the Gaza Strip, seven West Bank cities and part of an eighth to self-rule under peace deals launched in 1993. More than two million Palestinians live in the West Bank and Gaza, captured by Israel in a 1967 war.

"The secret map which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intends to present to the Palestinian Authority in final-status negotiations would give them less than 40 percent of the area," Haaretz military commentator Ze'ev Schiff said in the report, adding that the "Netanyahu map" was open to negotiation.

"The Palestinians will be told all the same that if the security situation will allow it over time, some security arrangements will be eased, and thus will the Palestinian entity get additional territories in the West Bank," Haaretz said.
Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported that as much as 60 percent of the West Bank would be turned over to the PLO under a military proposal presented to the cabinet ministers.
Asked which newspaper report to believe, Netanyahu told Israeli army radio: "I suggest that you not always believe what you read in the newspapers.
"I didn't specify any number," he said and added: "I have my own ideas." He said the discussion which began in the inner cabinet on Wednesday would continue in future meetings.

Tibi called the proposal published by Haaretz "a shot with automatic fire at the dying body of the Oslo accord" which launched Israeli-PLO peace moves four years ago: "Benjamin Netanyahu is successfully destroying this process," he said.

For all the Palestinian anger at anything short of an independent state, the reported map appeared to represent another nail in the coffin of a right-wing religious dream of a Jewish state in all of biblical Israel.
Haaretz said about half of Netanyahu's cabinet ministers backed the proposal to cede 40 percent of the West Bank.
National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon said the map, as reported, was little different from one he had conceived nearly 20 years ago.
